extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and advanced students interested in the Riemann zeta function and the Riemann hypothesis
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and survey of definitions, empirical laws, conjectures, heuristic frameworks, and arguments for/against the Riemann hypothesis focused on the nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function (Gram points, Gram's law, random-matrix analogies, numerical verification, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Gram point (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Gram point is a point on the critical line 1/2 + it where the zeta function is real and non-zero; usually numbered g_n where g_n is the unique solution of θ(t) = nπ, with θ the Riemann–Siegel theta function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gram points can be computed fairly easily by inverting the formula for θ. They are used to compare expected and actual positions of zeros along the critical line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gram's law
rubrics_metrics.description: The observation (Gram's law) that there is often exactly one zero of the zeta function between any two consecutive Gram points; closely related statements include that (−1)^n Z(g_n) is usually positive, or that Z(t) usually has opposite sign at consecutive Gram points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gram's law is empirical and holds frequently for small heights but has failures (the first failure occurs at the 127th zero). It is a heuristic measure of how zeros 'track' their expected positions; exceptions are recorded (indices of 'bad' Gram points).

rubrics_metrics.name: Good and bad Gram points (sign test)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Gram point t is called good if the zeta function is positive at 1/2 + it; bad Gram points are those where Z has the 'wrong' sign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sequence of bad Gram point indices is known (e.g., 126, 134, 195, 211, ... — OEIS A114856). Classifying Gram points as good/bad is a diagnostic for local deviations from Gram's law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gram block (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Gram block is an interval bounded by two good Gram points such that all the Gram points between them are bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gram blocks are used in refined statements: even if individual Gram intervals fail to contain exactly one zero, a Gram block often contains the expected total number of zeros (equal to the number of Gram intervals in the block).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rosser's rule
rubrics_metrics.description: A refinement of Gram's law due to Rosser, Yohe & Schoenfeld (1969): Gram blocks often have the expected number of zeros in them (the same as the number of Gram intervals), even though some individual Gram intervals may not have exactly one zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rosser et al. checked no exceptions to this rule in the first 3 million zeros, but there are infinitely many exceptions overall. Use Rosser's rule as a weaker, block-level expectation rather than a guarantee for each interval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of zero displacement by S(T)
rubrics_metrics.description: The distance of a zero from its expected position is controlled by the function S(T); S(T) grows extremely slowly with average size of order (log log T)^{1/2}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because S(T) is very slowly growing, Gram's law and Rosser's rule hold most of the time for small T but break down increasingly often at larger heights. This gives a quantitative explanation for why numerical checks at accessible heights may not reveal typical long-range behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-run statistical proportions for zeros in Gram intervals
rubrics_metrics.description: It is expected that asymptotically about 66% of Gram intervals contain exactly one zero, about 17% contain no zero, and about 17% contain two zeros (Hanga 2020).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These proportions summarize refined probabilistic behavior of zeros relative to Gram points; they indicate that Gram's law holds only in a fraction of intervals in the long run and provide targets for statistical/computational verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Random matrix theory analogy (GUE/pair correlation)
rubrics_metrics.description: After suitable rescaling to account for increasing density of zeros with height, the conjectured pair correlation function of the critical zeros agrees with that of eigenvalues in the Gaussian unitary ensemble (GUE) of random Hermitian matrices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This analogy (originating with Montgomery and tested numerically by Odlyzko) extends beyond nearest-neighbor spacings to higher correlation functions and is viewed as strong heuristic evidence that zeros follow the same local statistics as random matrices; it motivates thinking of zeros as eigenvalues of a selfadjoint operator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Random-matrix heuristic for moments and ratios (Keating & Snaith)
rubrics_metrics.description: A conjectural picture using averages over random unitary matrices predicts main constants in asymptotic moment formulas for |ζ(1/2 + it)|^{2k} as T→∞, separating a universal random-matrix factor from an arithmetic Euler-product factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These predictions have influenced later work on moments and ratios of L-functions; they provide quantitative conjectures to test numerically and theoretically against zeta-function behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Katz–Sarnak symmetry types for families of L-functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Katz & Sarnak proposed that families of L-functions have symmetry types governed by compact classical groups (unitary, orthogonal, symplectic), and that distributions of low-lying zeros should match the corresponding random-matrix ensembles; for the Riemann zeta function the relevant ensemble is the unitary group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a framework for predicting statistics of zeros in families and connects arithmetic data to symmetry types; it refines random-matrix predictions to families rather than isolated L-functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogues proved for other zeta/L-functions (theoretical evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several analogues of the Riemann hypothesis have been proved (e.g., Deligne's proof for varieties over finite fields, Selberg zeta functions; Goss zeta function proved by Sheats), providing theoretical reasons in favor of RH.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such positive results are considered evidence because they show the phenomenon holds in closely related settings, though counterexamples (e.g., some Epstein zeta functions without Euler product) show the situation is subtle and dependent on structural properties like Euler products and automorphicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical verification as evidence and its limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Large-scale computations have verified many zeros lie on the critical line to very high heights (Odlyzko, Gourdon, Platt & Trudgian, distributed projects like ZetaGrid), and these are often cited as strong evidence for RH.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerical evidence is persuasive but not decisive: slow-growing functions like log log T can hide eventual counterexamples at astronomically large heights (Skewes-type phenomena). Computations verify patterns up to reachable heights and can test statistical conjectures (e.g., GUE statistics) but cannot prove RH.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denjoy's probabilistic argument / Möbius function equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: Denjoy's probabilistic argument observes that if μ(n) behaved like a random sequence of ±1 then the partial sums M(x)=∑_{n≤x} μ(n) would satisfy M(x)=O(x^{1/2+ε}) with probability 1; the Riemann hypothesis is equivalent to such a bound for the Möbius function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives an intuitive probabilistic heuristic (μ behaving like coin tosses) for RH, but such arguments are hard to make rigorous and can mislead in some number-theoretic contexts (e.g., Maier's theorem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lehmer's phenomenon (close zeros) as interpretive data point
rubrics_metrics.description: Lehmer's phenomenon, where two zeros are sometimes very close, has been cited as a reason to disbelieve RH by some, but Odlyzko's computations suggest nearby pairs occur as often as predicted by Montgomery's conjecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Close zeros are not definitive evidence against RH: they can occur naturally under the random-matrix/statistical models consistent with RH; interpret such phenomena in light of predicted spacing statistics rather than as standalone refutations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of rigorous computational checks and algorithm verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Computational work (Odlyzko, Gourdon, Platt & Trudgian, van de Lune et al.) both computes zeros at very large heights and verifies previous computations, e.g., checking algorithms like Odlyzko–Schönhage and verifying earlier results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rigorous computation and cross-checking provide validation of numerical evidence and of algorithms used to locate zeros; they can demonstrate consistency with statistical conjectures and detect exceptions to empirical laws (Gram, Rosser) within the computed range.
